video_title: Disney: The Renaissance and the Empire
gist: A 4.5-hour business history of the Walt Disney Company from the 1984 Eisner-Wells boardroom coup through the Disney Renaissance, the accidental ESPN cash machine inside the 1995 Cap Cities/ABC deal, Iger's Pixar/Marvel/Lucasfilm/Fox roll-up, and the Disney+ pivot. The hosts' core argument: ESPN's affiliate-fee geyser (not the famous flywheel) funded everything, streaming is a structurally worse business than the cable bundle plus theatrical/home-video windows it replaced, and today parks and cruises throw off ~60% of company operating income while theatrical distribution is only 3% of revenue.

insights.claim: Disney in 1983-84 was a break-up candidate whose stock fell from $82 to $52 and which was worth more sold for parts than run as a going concern, forcing management to dilute shareholders and sell ~25% of the company to the Bass family as a friendly white-knight block against corporate raiders.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: The template for defeating a raider by manufacturing a friendly control block is still the playbook for cornered boards; it also created a concentrated holder whose forced selling later destabilized the CEO.
insights.quote: Their stock dropped from $82 to $52 that the company was worth more if you sold it for parts than actually running it.

insights.claim: By 1984 Disney's creative engine was economically dead: parks and consumer products threw off roughly a quarter billion dollars of profit while film and TV contributed about $2 million, meaning the IP flywheel at the center of the company had stopped turning.
insights.speaker: Ben Gilbert
insights.so_what: A useful diagnostic: when a franchise business's content P&L goes to zero, the durable asset (parks, licensing) masks decay for years before it shows up in the financials.
insights.quote: In 1984, Disney generated a quarter billion dollars of profit from its parks and consumer products and a mere$2 million from film and TV.

insights.claim: Eisner and Diller's 'singles and doubles / high concept' strategy at Paramount deliberately underweighted A-list talent and overweighted script and concept quality, and Eisner leaked a memo codifying it as a commercial rather than artistic mandate.
insights.speaker: Acquired host (quoting Michael Eisner's memo)
insights.so_what: The same cost-discipline-plus-concept framework is the underwriting logic for any hit-driven, power-law business: buy the option cheaply and let story quality, not star salaries, drive returns.
insights.quote: We have no obligation to make art. We have no obligation to make history. We have no obligation to make a statement. But to make money, it is often important to make history, to make art, or to make some significant statement.

insights.claim: Katzenberg's corollary to high concept is that star power only buys an opening weekend, not sustained performance, which justifies paying up for scripts rather than casts.
insights.speaker: Acquired host (quoting Jeffrey Katzenberg's memo)
insights.so_what: A cost-allocation rule for any content business: spend on the durable asset (story/IP), not the rented one (talent), because rented inputs do not compound.
insights.quote: celebrity can open a film, but celebrity can't carry a film

insights.claim: The single highest-ROI move of the Eisner-Wells era was raising Disney park and parking prices that had been frozen since Walt's death through a decade of 1970s inflation, because in a fixed-cost operating business every incremental dollar of price falls straight to the bottom line.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Screen for consumer businesses with structurally under-priced assets and no demand elasticity — repricing is the cheapest free cash flow in any operating turnaround.
insights.quote: I mean, you can criticize them all you want today for raising prices, but they had I don't know 5 to 10x of you can raise the price and it wouldn't impact demand for a second back then.

insights.claim: Disney's live-action revival under Eisner produced a hit rate of 27 profitable films out of the first 33, an outlier in a business the hosts describe as power-law distributed like venture capital or book publishing.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: An 82% hit rate in a power-law business is the signature of a repeatable process edge, not luck — the same test to apply to any studio or fund claiming a system.
insights.quote: All told, 27 of their first 33 movies that they make are profitable, which in Hollywood to have a hit rate like that, that's like making 33 venture capital investments and only losing money on six of them

insights.claim: Eisner's team financed its entire eight-year, 75-film slate through an outside partner, Silver Screen, rather than from Disney's own balance sheet, because the park price increases alone could not fund the studio ramp.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Off-balance-sheet slate financing let Disney keep the upside on IP while outsourcing production risk — a structure that still defines film finance.

insights.claim: Disney's operating profit went from well under $300 million in 1984 to just under $2 billion a decade later and its market cap hit $22 billion by 1994, a 10x that made it the most valuable traditional media company, ahead of Time Warner, Viacom and News Corp.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Benchmark for what an operational turnaround plus IP revival can do to a media multiple — and the high-water mark against which all later Disney management is judged.

insights.claim: The Disney Renaissance was created less by executives than by two Broadway imports, lyricist Howard Ashman and composer Alan Menken, whose insight was to convert animated features from cartoons-with-songs into structurally proper stage musicals.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Value in creative businesses often concentrates in one or two non-obvious individual hires; identify the specific creative input, not the org chart, when underwriting a content revival.
insights.quote: Howard when he hears the word Disney instantly says, I want to work in animation. I feel there is a connection between animation and musical theater.

insights.claim: Ashman's reusable story formula was the 'I want' song: the leading lady sits down in the third number and tells the audience exactly what she wants, and the rest of the film is the audience rooting for her to get it.
insights.speaker: Acquired host (quoting Howard Ashman)
insights.so_what: A transferable narrative template that turned an unreliable hit business into a repeatable one — the closest thing to a manufacturing process in animation.
insights.quote: Well, in every great Broadway musical, the third song, the leading lady goes and she sits on something. Might be a rock, might be a trash can, and she sings a song to the world, telling the audience what she wants.

insights.claim: The Little Mermaid was a modest theatrical performer that was out-grossed by When Harry Met Sally in 1989, and only became a cultural and financial phenomenon when the VHS release in 1990 let children rewatch it on demand.
insights.speaker: Acquired host (quoting Ben Cohen, WSJ)
insights.so_what: Box office is a poor proxy for IP value when a repeat-consumption channel exists — the same logic that now makes streaming placement, not opening weekend, the value driver.
insights.quote: Once upon a time, Disney movies got beat at the box office by romcoms. The Little Mermaid made less money than when Harry Met Sally in 1989.

insights.claim: Renaissance-era animation delivered extraordinary unit economics: Beauty and the Beast grossed $330 million on a $25 million production budget, Aladdin about $500 million on $28 million, and The Lion King $750 million on $45 million.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: 10x-plus gross-to-budget ratios are the historical baseline Disney is now compared against, against today's rumored $700 million all-in tentpoles.

insights.claim: Disney kept animation budgets low during the Renaissance by investing roughly $10 million of fixed cost in CAPS, a computer-animated production system that eliminated inking and painting and simulated an unlimited-plane multiplane camera.
insights.speaker: Ben Gilbert
insights.so_what: A small fixed-cost technology investment converted a variable-cost craft into a scalable one — the clearest example in the episode of capex buying gross margin.

insights.claim: Pixar's first paying customer was Disney: the initial check to Pixar Inc. was for building the CAPS system, and Pixar software also rendered the 3D ballroom background in Beauty and the Beast, Disney's first use of 3D animation in a film.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: The eventual acquirer's most important asset began as a vendor relationship — a reminder to watch which suppliers are quietly learning your business.

insights.claim: The talent that rebuilt both Disney and Pixar was concentrated in a single CalArts classroom that Walt Disney had endowed with half his estate as a talent pipeline — Lasseter, Brad Bird, Tim Burton, Musker, Stanton, Brenda Chapman and Pete Docter — and Disney hired then fired nearly all of them.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Institutional talent pipelines can pay off decades later and outside the sponsoring company — a strong argument for valuing founder-built institutions, and a warning about mismanaging them.

insights.claim: Disney's post-1994 animation collapse — Pocahontas through Atlantis, Treasure Planet, Home on the Range and Chicken Little — took years to show up in the financials because parks and consumer products monetize IP on a long lag.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: In IP businesses, creative decay is a leading indicator that reported earnings will lag by five to ten years — watch the slate, not the segment P&L.
insights.quote: Because they don't make most of their money from actual profits at the box office when the movie comes out the first time, there's a delayed impact to animation sucking that doesn't show up in the financials until way later.

themes.theme: Flywheel Extensions: Home Video, Retail, Broadway, Resorts

insights.claim: Home video was the single most profitable Disney innovation of the 1980s: a deliberately limited 1.7 million-unit VHS run of Pinocchio at $29.95 sold out instantly for about $50 million of gross sales at near-zero incremental cost, and Disney reportedly kept $17-$20 per tape.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: A textbook case of monetizing an existing library through a new distribution window at ~60-70% incremental margin, with no new production cost.

insights.claim: Home video did not cannibalize theatrical re-releases because tapes broke and were lost, so ownership increased rather than satisfied demand — Cinderella did $34 million in a re-release plus 6 million VHS units for about $200 million of combined gross.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: The cannibalization fear that blocks new distribution channels is often wrong; test whether the new channel deepens rather than substitutes demand.

insights.claim: Home video re-rated the entire economics of animation, turning it into the second-largest profit center at Disney after parks and making any animation budget justifiable: Aladdin sold 30 million tapes (~$900 million) and The Lion King 32 million (~$1 billion) at roughly 50%+ cash flow margin.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: When a second monetization window carries ~50% margins, greenlight thresholds collapse — precisely the dynamic that has now reversed as physical media disappeared.
insights.quote: Having a home video release channel instantly makes whatever you want to spend on animation worth it.

insights.claim: The Lion King stage musical has grossed over $11 billion across 30 years of Broadway plus touring, which the hosts argue makes it the highest-grossing single piece of entertainment in any medium — averaging about $350 million of gross revenue a year, the equivalent of an extra hit film annually.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Live adaptation is the most underrated IP annuity in media — decades of high-priced, non-decaying cash flow from a single story, with no content treadmill.
insights.quote: The Lion King musical has grossed over $11 billion in total revenue in its run, which I think makes it the single highest grossing entertainment product in history in any medium.

insights.claim: Disney built more than 750 retail stores in American malls in the 1990s, creating a weekly physical touchpoint that compounded with home video to embed the brand in a single generation of children.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Distribution density at the child level is what creates the multi-generational brand annuity; the store closures after 9/11 marked the first break in that loop.

insights.claim: Eisner's biggest structural change to parks was converting them from day-trip theme parks into multi-day resorts — Grand Floridian, Swan, Dolphin, the Vacation Club timeshare, Hollywood Studios and Animal Kingdom — moving the competitive set from a Saturday ballgame to a European vacation.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Redefining the competitive set is how you move a consumer from a $300 to a $3,000 wallet share; the same logic underwrites today's $60 billion parks and cruise capex.
insights.quote: They changed the park from something that could compete with going to a baseball game on a Saturday to something that could compete with your European 5day vacation.

insights.claim: Euro Disney cost $4 billion, lost money for years and required a rebrand to Disneyland Paris plus product changes, showing that Disney's park model does not port internationally without local adaptation and macro timing.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: A caution flag for the announced Abu Dhabi park and for any operator assuming a domestic experience concept exports cleanly.

insights.claim: The 1990s extension playbook — home video, mall retail, Broadway, resort conversion — is what the hosts credit for the era's outperformance, and they argue much of it is structurally unavailable to today's management.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: If the surplus channels of that era are gone, comparing current Disney management to the 1990s is a category error — judge them on parks pricing and streaming scale instead.
insights.quote: Home video, Broadway, the stores in the malls, the parks, and transforming Walt Disney World into a resort.

insights.claim: The 1993 FCC repeal of the Financial Interest and Syndication rules, which had barred networks from owning their programming, is what made the studio-network combinations of the mid-1990s including Disney/Cap Cities possible.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Regulatory repeal, not strategy fashion, opened the M&A window — a reminder that deal waves in media are usually policy-triggered.

insights.claim: Disney acquired Capital Cities/ABC for $19 billion in 1995, the second-largest acquisition in history at the time behind RJR Nabisco, in a deal negotiated primarily with Warren Buffett, whose Berkshire Hathaway was Cap Cities' largest shareholder.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: The buried asset (ESPN), not the headline asset (ABC), carried the return — the standard argument for underwriting conglomerate deals asset by asset.

insights.claim: Neither Disney nor Eisner understood at the time that ESPN was the prize: it had 66 million subscribers and an average affiliate fee still under a dollar a month, with essentially all of its pricing leverage ahead of it.
insights.speaker: Acquired host (quoting Roy E. Disney)
insights.so_what: The best acquisitions in media history were partly accidental; the repeatable lesson is to buy assets with untapped pricing power rather than proven earnings.
insights.quote: Nobody would have told you when that deal, the ABC deal, was being made that ESPN was going to turn out to be the weightlifter of the group.

insights.claim: ESPN invented the affiliate-fee business model for cable — before it, channels either sold ads only or paid operators for carriage — and then used long-dated exclusive sports rights as the leverage to raise carriage rates roughly 20% per renegotiation under credible threat of pulling the signal.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: The mechanism is the model: exclusive must-have content plus consumer outrage risk equals contractual pricing power — and it inverts the moment the rights become contestable.
insights.quote: sports rights are the biggest point of leverage that they could possibly have over the cable operators

insights.claim: ESPN commands by far the highest affiliate fee of any cable channel — the hosts cite roughly three to four times the next highest and a figure the auto-captions render as '$942 per month per subscriber' (i.e., about $9.42) — producing billions of dollars of near-contractually-guaranteed monthly cash flow.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Quantifies the single largest source of Disney's historical free cash flow and the size of the hole cord-cutting is now opening.
insights.quote: I know it's the single highest paid channel by like 3x 4x.

insights.claim: Owning ESPN let Disney bundle-negotiate its weaker channels — Disney Channel, A&E, Lifetime — into higher carriage rates alongside ESPN, a bundle within the bundle.
insights.speaker: Ben Gilbert
insights.so_what: Tie-in pricing off one must-have asset is how portfolio media companies extracted value; losing the must-have collapses the whole tier's pricing.

insights.claim: Disney's cable networks segment — roughly three-quarters ESPN by analyst estimates — accounted for 60% of the entire company's operating income between 2008 and 2011, over $5 billion of profit, meaning Disney had effectively become a cable affiliate-fee company.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Reframes a decade of Disney's reported earnings quality: the branded content story was funded by a bundled utility-like toll, not by the flywheel.
insights.quote: That segment accounted for 60% of the entire company's operating income during that 2008 to 2011 period.

insights.claim: Ben Thompson's framing, endorsed by the hosts, is that the cable bundle was scalable in a way Walt's flywheel never could be because nearly every US household paid every month regardless of whether Disney had a hit — making the classic Disney model a side business to the real money maker.
insights.speaker: Acquired host (quoting Ben Thompson)
insights.so_what: The central contrarian claim of the episode: the celebrated IP flywheel was not the profit engine, which reframes how to value Disney's IP versus its distribution.
insights.quote: Walt Disney's chart, the famous flywheel one, may have been a very satisfying business model, but the reality of Disney's TV business is that it was scalable in a way that the Disney chart could never be.

insights.claim: The Cap Cities acquisition permanently cost Disney its strategic clarity by bolting an advertising and affiliate-fee business with non-evergreen, mostly third-party content onto an evergreen IP flywheel — two incompatible operating models under one roof.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Explains both the Ovitz failure and the recurring Wall Street pressure to spin ESPN — conglomerates of incompatible business models carry a permanent management and multiple discount.
insights.quote: Disney never again would get to be just Disney.

insights.claim: A 20% minority stake in ESPN sold to Hearst in the RJR Nabisco/KKR fallout has generated billions of dollars of free cash flow for Hearst over four decades with no operating involvement, and Hearst still owns it today.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: One of the great passive minority stakes in media history — a reminder that non-control positions in monopoly assets can outperform operating businesses.

insights.claim: ESPN could offset cord-cutting with price increases until roughly 2023, when subscriber declines finally outpaced affiliate fee increases and revenue began falling into 2024 — the point at which cable and ESPN entered their endgame.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Marks the specific year the price/volume offset broke — the timing input for any ESPN spin or terminal-value model.

insights.claim: Sports rights costs inverted ESPN's leverage: the Monday Night Football package went from $1.1 billion a year in 2006 to $1.9 billion in 2011 to $2.7 billion by 2021, even as viewership rose, because value in the chain shifted from the middleman network to the leagues.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: A concrete rights-inflation curve; the beneficiary of live sports scarcity is the league, not the distributor.

insights.claim: Tech platforms now outbid ESPN for sports rights because they have more ways to monetize the same viewer — Amazon converts an NFL viewer into a Prime subscriber — and in any auction the price is set by whoever can structurally monetize best.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: A general rule for competitive bidding in any market: the widest monetization surface wins the asset, which is why ESPN won for 30 years and now loses.
insights.quote: The price is set by the highest bidder. And if somebody has a business model that structurally can outmonetize what you can, then they're going to win and the price is going to be set by them.

insights.claim: As online content becomes abundant, the scarcity premium on shared live cultural experiences rises — visible in World Cup, Taylor Swift and Super Bowl ticket prices — which trickles down into higher sports rights fees.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: A durable secular bid under live sports and live events pricing, independent of the cable bundle's decline.
insights.quote: there is an increasing return to shared cultural experiences happening live in a way that made sports way more important than they ever have been before

insights.claim: ESPN's differentiation eroded structurally because social media replaced its highlights monopoly, so if the only remaining reason to subscribe is the game itself, excess profits accrue permanently to the rights holders rather than the network.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: The mechanism by which a distribution monopoly becomes a pass-through: watch whether any network can rebuild differentiated surround content.

insights.claim: ESPN cannot build its own flywheel because sports content has almost no shelf life — nobody rewatches last season's ManningCast — so unlike Disney IP it can never accumulate a library asset, making it a stabilizing but declining asset.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Separates the two asset types inside Disney: predictable but non-compounding sports cash flow versus lumpy but compounding IP — they warrant different multiples.
insights.quote: Sports have a very limited shelf life. You are not going back and watching Manning cast episodes from last season.

insights.claim: Disney carved ESPN into its own reporting segment in October 2023, which the hosts read as creating optionality to spin it out in response to Wall Street pressure — even though ESPN still produces about $3 billion a year in operating income.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Segment reporting changes are a leading indicator of structural separation; a $3 billion-profit 'declining asset' is a live spin candidate.

insights.claim: The 2025 deal trading the NFL Network into ESPN for a 10% stake in ESPN aligns both parties: the NFL exits a business outside its competency while gaining an incentive to keep ESPN a viable bidder for its own rights.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Equity-for-assets swaps between a supplier and its largest customer are a way to prop up a bidder you need alive — a structure worth watching across other leagues.

insights.claim: ESPN Unlimited at $30 a month is aggressively bundled with Disney+ and Hulu for an extra $6 not just for reach but for churn mitigation, because bundle subscribers churn at materially lower rates than single-service subscribers.
insights.speaker: Ben Gilbert
insights.so_what: Bundling is now a retention tool, not just an acquisition tool — the single most important lever in subscription video unit economics.
insights.quote: the bundle subscribers churn at a much lower rate than any individual streaming service cuz you're not thinking that hard about how much value am I getting out of this particular app this month

themes.theme: Eisner's Unraveling and the Iger Succession

insights.claim: Three shocks in 1994 broke the Eisner management system: Frank Wells died in a helicopter crash, Eisner had emergency quadruple bypass surgery months later, and Katzenberg quit after being denied the number two job, later settling his bonus lawsuit for a reported $280 million.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Key-person and succession risk is the underpriced variable in founder- or duo-led companies; Disney's decade-long decline traces to a single year of it.

insights.claim: Katzenberg's exit created Disney's first full-stack competitor in DreamWorks, which poached Disney animators including Lion King head of story Brenda Chapman, raised Disney's animation cost structure by bidding for talent, and produced Shrek at roughly half a billion dollars of box office.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Departing executives who can replicate the model raise your input costs before they take your revenue — watch wage inflation as the first sign of competitive entry.

insights.claim: Hiring super-agent Michael Ovitz as president failed within 14 months and cost $140 million in severance because the agent skill set — being liked, saying yes, moving fast across hundreds of projects — is the inverse of the COO job of saying no and managing slow processes at scale.
insights.speaker: Ben Gilbert
insights.so_what: A reusable screen for executive hires: match the job's actual daily operating requirements, not the candidate's prestige or adjacent-industry success.
insights.quote: The job of being an agent is being liked, saying yes, wielding your power, making things happen quick, being involved in 15 projects at once

insights.claim: September 11 hit Disney at its most vulnerable point: parks revenue went to near zero, the stock fell nearly 25%, most mall retail stores were closed, and the Bass family faced a margin call forcing them to dump about $2 billion of Disney shares, wiping out Eisner's largest shareholder support.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Forced selling by a concentrated supportive holder is a governance risk multiplier — an exogenous shock converted an operating problem into a control fight.

insights.claim: Roy E. Disney and Stanley Gold pioneered the public grassroots shareholder campaign with SaveDisney.com in 2003, delivering a 43% withhold vote against Eisner at the March 2004 meeting after ISS-type advisers and CalPERS backed them.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: A 43% withhold vote is effectively terminal for a CEO — a useful threshold when handicapping activist campaigns.

insights.claim: Comcast's surprise $54 billion all-stock hostile bid for Disney in February 2004 was motivated substantially by the chance to own ESPN, its most powerful supplier and annual carriage-fee adversary; the bid collapsed when Comcast's stock fell and Disney's rose.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Vertical acquirers bid for suppliers with pricing power over them; ESPN's leverage was so large it made a cable operator try to buy all of Disney.

insights.claim: At the time of the Comcast bid, Disney's cable networks generated $2 billion of operating income against $4.5 billion companywide — nearly 50% of total profits from what was effectively ESPN.
insights.speaker: Ben Gilbert
insights.so_what: Quantifies why the bid happened and why any ESPN spin-out debate is really a debate about half of Disney's historical earnings power.

insights.claim: Bob Iger won the CEO job by reframing the contest away from his record as the incumbent's number two toward three forward-looking pillars: high-quality branded content, embracing technology rather than fighting it, and global expansion into China and India.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Those three pillars explain every subsequent Disney capital allocation decision — Pixar/Marvel/Lucasfilm, BAMTech/Disney+, and the Fox India assets.

insights.claim: Iger's second pillar was genuinely contrarian for 2005 because the rest of traditional media was suing technology companies rather than partnering with them, with Viacom about to sue YouTube and the music industry's Napster experience fresh.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: The posture toward disruptive distribution — partner versus litigate — separated the one traditional media company that stayed independent from the ones that did not.

insights.claim: Eisner's 21-year tenure produced roughly a 20-25x market cap increase (about $2 billion to roughly $50 billion), revenue growth from $1.7 billion to $31 billion (a 15% CAGR) and net income from $97 million to $2.5 billion, with the hosts ranking ESPN as reasons one, two and three for his success and the Renaissance only fourth.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: A quantified reminder that the acquisition, not the creative revival, drove the shareholder return — the same test to apply to Iger's record.
insights.quote: ESPN is arguments one, two, and three of why was he a great CEO?

themes.theme: Pixar: Leverage, IPO Timing, and the $7.4B Deal

insights.claim: Steve Jobs bought the Lucasfilm computer graphics group for a $5 million check to George Lucas plus a $5 million check into the new entity, owning 70% with employees holding 30%, and Lucas only sold because he needed cash for a divorce without giving up Lucasfilm equity.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Motivated sellers create the best entry prices; the entire Pixar-Disney outcome traces to a personal liquidity need unrelated to the asset's value.

insights.claim: The original Toy Story contract was punitive for Pixar: Disney funded the roughly $30 million budget and marketing, kept all IP and sequel rights, granted Pixar under 10% of profits after marketing recoupment, and excluded sequels from the three-picture count.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: The financier who supplies capital and distribution captures the IP; Pixar's entire later strategy was about buying its way out of that structural position.

insights.claim: Pixar's core process edge is the story reel — a cheap 2D, temp-dialogue cut of the whole film iterated roughly eight times before any 3D work — which Jobs described as beta testing the movie and credited for a structurally higher hit rate.
insights.speaker: Acquired host (quoting Steve Jobs and John Lasseter)
insights.so_what: A transferable de-risking method for any high-fixed-cost creative product: build the cheapest possible full-fidelity prototype and kill or fix it before committing capital.
insights.quote: in essence, it lets us beta test and iterate on our films before we actually make it. We believe it's one of the reasons that the hit rate can be substantially different.

insights.claim: Computer animation is not a cheaper substitute for 2D but a categorically different and more expensive activity — building and computing an entire virtual universe frame by frame, at an hour or two per frame and about three and a half minutes of footage per week on a 117-machine Sun render farm.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Explains why animation costs did not fall with technology and why compute-intensive content pipelines carry very different capital requirements than they appear to.
insights.quote: 2D animation is art. It's like you're painting a picture. What Pixar does is they are creating a universe and then they are calculating every atom of that universe.

insights.claim: Jobs deliberately sequenced Pixar's IPO for the week after Toy Story's release specifically to raise the capital needed to fund 50% of future production budgets and thereby win negotiating leverage over Disney — a series of consecutive bet-the-company moves.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Capital raised at the moment of maximum narrative is not vanity — it is the direct input to bargaining power over a distribution partner.

insights.claim: Toy Story grossed nearly $400 million worldwide and was the highest-grossing film of the year, and Pixar's IPO a week later closed at a $1.5 billion market cap on a $140 million raise — the largest IPO of the year, bigger than Netscape — making Jobs, who held 78%, a billionaire.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Pixar, not Apple, is where Jobs made his fortune — and the proceeds are what converted Pixar from contractor to peer.
insights.quote: Pixar alone made Steve Jobs a billionaire on IPO day.

insights.claim: The renegotiated post-Toy Story deal was nominally 50/50 but effectively about 65/35 in Disney's favor once the distribution fee was applied, and Jobs's later grievance was learning that Lucas's distribution terms with Fox were better than Pixar's with Disney.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Distribution fees are where headline splits get eroded; benchmark them against the best comparable deal, not the counterparty's first offer.

insights.claim: Toy Story 2 overturned Disney's long-standing doctrine that sequels must go direct-to-video and would always be inferior; released theatrically it grossed almost $500 million, teaching Disney that franchise sequels are a valuable business model — the inversion that defines the industry today.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: The origin of the sequel-first industry model — and, per the hosts' later bear case, the origin of IP over-exploitation risk.

insights.claim: Eisner wrote a board memo predicting Finding Nemo would flop and calling it a useful reality check that would improve Disney's negotiating leverage over Pixar; the memo leaked, Nemo grossed $871 million theatrically and sold about 65 million DVDs at roughly $30 for roughly $3 billion of combined gross, and the relationship became irreparable.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Rooting against a partner in whose economics you hold the majority is a governance tell; here it cost Disney the most valuable partnership in its history for two years.
insights.quote: he's seen the Nemo reel. It's a bad movie. It's going to flop and it'll be a quote reality check for those guys and it'll be great for Disney's negotiating leverage for Pixar to fail.

insights.claim: Around 2003 the LA Times reported Pixar films accounted for as much as half of Disney studio operating income, at the same time Disney's own animation was releasing Treasure Planet and Atlantis — so Pixar's final demand (100% of profits, a 10% distribution fee, and relinquishing co-ownership of past films) was made from a position of genuine strength.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Supplier concentration risk: when one partner supplies half your segment profit, contract renewal becomes an existential negotiation.
insights.quote: Steve and Pixar did get a reality check. And the reality check is that they don't need Disney at all.

insights.claim: Iger's winning move was offering not just to buy Pixar for $7.4 billion in newly issued stock but to hand Lasseter and Catmull control of Disney Animation itself, with Pixar kept fully intact in Emeryville and Jobs becoming Disney's largest shareholder at roughly 7.7%.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: The acquisition premium was paid for management, not assets — the rare deal where the acquirer explicitly surrendered its core division to the target's leadership.
insights.quote: my predecessor burned the bridge. I'd like to buy you. I'm basically open to any price.

insights.claim: The hosts conclude Pixar could never have become a standalone Disney competitor despite winning creatively, because it had no business operators other than Jobs and Jobs knew he was dying — which is why he sold and why he later toasted that the deal saved two companies.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Creative excellence without commercial leadership is not a durable independent business — the test to apply to any studio, label or game developer weighing independence.
insights.quote: Look what we did. we saved two companies.

insights.claim: The Toy Story franchise alone has done over $4 billion at the box office and roughly $30 billion in lifetime retail sales, which at Disney's ~5% licensing rate implies about $3.5 billion of high-margin revenue — well over half the effective $6.4 billion ex-cash purchase price, before parks, Disney+ or home video contribution.
insights.speaker: Ben Gilbert
insights.so_what: A clean franchise-level payback model for IP acquisitions: box office plus a licensing royalty on retail gross, with parks and streaming as free option value.

insights.claim: The vast majority of the top 15 titles viewed weekly on Disney+ are Pixar or post-2005 Disney Animation films rather than live action, Star Wars or Marvel — kids rewatch Frozen, Encanto, Moana and Zootopia, not Snow White.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: The strongest single justification for the Pixar price and the clearest signal of which IP actually drives streaming retention and downstream parks demand.
insights.quote: We've heard that the vast majority of the top 15 movies viewed every week on Disney Plus are either Pixar or Disney animation.

themes.theme: Iger's IP Roll-Up: Marvel, Lucasfilm, Fox

insights.claim: Disney's $4 billion Marvel purchase in 2009 was contrarian because the best characters were already licensed away — X-Men to Fox, Spider-Man to Sony — leaving buyers unclear what they were acquiring; by 2025 the MCU had become the most successful film franchise in history at nearly $32 billion of box office across 37 films.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: The value was in the world-building capability and the residual character set, not the marquee characters — a case for buying creative teams with a system rather than named assets.
insights.quote: So, what are you even buying when you're buying Marvel?

insights.claim: The hosts frame all three Iger acquisitions as the same thesis executed three times — find great stories and storytellers and give them a bigger canvas — and note Iger recognized A+ franchise IP with running room before others and paid up with stock.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: A repeatable acquisition screen: durable multi-generational IP plus a creative team that has not yet had scale distribution behind it.
insights.quote: there are great stories and storytellers here and let's give them a bigger canvas to paint on

insights.claim: Lucasfilm at $4 billion in 2012 was correctly cheaper than Pixar because it had no films in production, but the hosts argue in hindsight Disney should have paid well below what it paid for Marvel because Star Wars had far less exploitation runway and was executed poorly.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Franchise breadth (number of viable stories and characters) matters more than franchise fame in pricing IP — Star Wars's mythic status did not translate into Marvel-scale output.

insights.claim: ESPN's cable profits funded the entire IP roll-up: Pixar at $7.4 billion was about 2.5 years of cable profit, Marvel about one year of 2009 cable profit and Lucasfilm well under a year — roughly four years of ESPN cash bought all three.
insights.speaker: Ben Gilbert
insights.so_what: The Buffett-style framing the hosts use: harvest cash from a business that cannot reinvest and redeploy into ones that can — and the corollary risk when the cash producer stops producing.
insights.quote: ESPN paid for Pixar, Marvel, and Lucasfilm

insights.claim: The revived flywheel showed up in consumer products and music: Disney sold three million Elsa and Anna dresses in Frozen's first year, was doing over $50 billion a year in gross retail merchandise sales by 2015 (nearly 2x in five years), and the Frozen soundtrack was the best-selling album of 2014 at 10 million copies, beating Taylor Swift's 1989.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Retail gross and soundtrack performance are the cleanest real-time indicators of IP health — and Frozen may be the last time Disney hit those levels with new IP.

insights.claim: Over Iger's first decade parks revenue nearly doubled and parks operating income nearly tripled, company revenue grew from $32 billion to $52 billion, operating income from $4.7 billion to $14.7 billion, and market cap 4x from $50 billion to $200 billion.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Establishes that Iger's return came entirely in the first decade — the second decade was flat, which is the fact the bear case rests on.

insights.claim: Fox sold its entertainment library to Disney because its own analysis concluded the library's highest and best use was on someone else's streaming service — it kept first-run value assets like news and sports and went all-in on linear, the exact opposite of Disney's rewatchability strategy.
insights.speaker: Ben Gilbert
insights.so_what: A clean strategic bifurcation: rewatchable catalog belongs in streaming, perishable first-run content belongs in linear/live — a sorting rule for valuing any media library.
insights.quote: Disney's keep things that have high rewatchability and monetize them over and over.

insights.claim: Comcast's spoiler bid drove the Fox price from a best-and-final $52 billion to $71.3 billion — a free $19 billion to Fox shareholders — and even after $14 billion of regional sports network and $15 billion of Sky divestitures, the effective ~$44 billion price makes Fox the worst of Disney's big acquisitions, with the India assets later merged into Reliance at a fraction of the deal value.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: A cautionary case on auction dynamics and scale-driven M&A: the strategic rationale (library, Hulu control, India) did not justify a price equal to 40% of Disney's own market cap at the time.

insights.claim: The August 4, 2015 Disney earnings call where Iger disclosed modest ESPN subscriber losses was the ground zero event for traditional media: Disney's stock fell 10% the next day, Fox, Time Warner and Discovery had similar drawdowns and Viacom fell over 20%, even though ESPN still had 92 million subscribers after losing 3 million.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: The market repriced an entire sector off a single directional inflection in a previously monotonic metric — a template for how terminal-value narratives break.

insights.claim: Disney's stock price today is flat versus 11 years ago while the S&P 500 is up roughly 3.5x, meaning the market believes Disney's long-run future cash flows are worth no more now than in 2015.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: The single starkest performance fact in the episode and the framing for whether the streaming pivot destroyed or merely preserved value.
insights.quote: it's gone up and down, but it is flat to 11 years ago

insights.claim: Every major traditional media company except Disney has effectively become a vassal of the technology platforms — AT&T/Time Warner, Warner Bros. Discovery, Paramount/Skydance — and as of the 2026 recording only Netflix, YouTube and Disney generate large profit streams in film and TV.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Defines the surviving profit pool in Hollywood: two tech platforms plus one IP-and-parks company; everything else is consolidation supply.
insights.quote: all of these traditional media companies, with the exception of Disney, have basically all become kind of surfs in the streaming kingdoms of the technology companies of which Netflix and YouTube are actually the winners here

insights.claim: Disney bought its streaming capability rather than building it — a 33% BAMTech stake from MLB in 2016 with an option to control — after nearly acquiring Twitter, a deal Iger walked away from the night before signing.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: The buy-versus-build decision on core technology capability, and a near-miss that would have changed Disney's brand risk profile entirely.

insights.claim: Disney deliberately walked away from hundreds of millions of dollars a year of pure-profit Netflix licensing revenue — roughly 2% of companywide operating income — to start its own subscriber base from zero, a move only affordable because declining ESPN was still a cash bulwark.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Quantifies the opportunity cost of vertical integration in streaming and shows that the legacy cash cow was the enabling condition, not the obstacle.

insights.claim: Disney had to deliberately cripple ESPN's early direct-to-consumer product because the affiliate-fee model pays per subscriber regardless of viewership, whereas direct-to-consumer only monetizes actual watchers — bundling captures the casual fans and non-consumers that a $30 standalone ESPN never would.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: The core economics of why unbundling destroys value for must-have niche content: you trade a broad low-intensity payer base for a narrow high-intensity one.
insights.quote: the whole magic of the affiliate fee business model is you get paid a subscriber fee whether those subscribers watch the channel or not

insights.claim: Disney+ launched at $6.99 with 10 million signups in 24 hours and 26 million in the first quarter, then COVID accelerated it to 100 million subscribers in 16 months against a 5-year goal of 60-90 million, driving Disney's market cap to a $360 billion peak in March 2021 in a zero-rate market.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: The peak that anchored expectations; the hosts note the stock began falling back by October 2021, making 2021 a valuation artifact rather than a business inflection.

insights.claim: The fundamental strategic conflict is that streaming demands a constant fire hose of new content while Disney's brand and flywheel were built on scarce, infrequent, event-scale releases followed by long harvesting windows — the two operating models are orthogonal.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: The central analytical claim of the episode's back half: Disney's streaming losses were not just investment but a business-model mismatch that also damages the underlying IP.
insights.quote: streaming is the exact freaking opposite. It is every time I open that, there better be something new and fresh for me to consume.

insights.claim: Ben Gilbert's 2019 warning on Acquired proved correct: Disney underestimated how much content subscribers need to stay satiated, and back-catalog access alone would not sustain a $7-a-month subscription without an aggressive content fire hose.
insights.speaker: Ben Gilbert
insights.so_what: A confirmed prior that generalizes: library depth drives acquisition, but only new-release cadence drives retention in subscription video.
insights.quote: One reason to doubt it, it being Disney Plus, is I think Disney may be underestimating just how much content people need to stay satiated.

insights.claim: Disney faces asymmetric brand risk in streaming that Netflix does not: expanding differentiated universes to feed the content treadmill devalues the original IP, and a run of bombs erodes the Disney brand itself, whereas the Netflix brand carries no such expectation.
insights.speaker: Ben Gilbert
insights.so_what: Brand equity is a compounding asset that can be spent down by volume — a real cost that never appears in the streaming segment P&L.
insights.quote: The Netflix brand doesn't mean anything to anyone. The Netflix brand is the button that I push on my TV when I want to watch stuff.

insights.claim: Marvel's post-Endgame problems were structural, not just creative: Disney demanded roughly 50% more production to feed streaming immediately after a story that was designed to end, and the multiverse expansion retroactively made the original decade of stakes feel unimportant.
insights.speaker: Ben Gilbert
insights.so_what: The clearest case study of streaming volume destroying franchise value; the hosts say the post-2021 Marvel slate may be net negative on theatrical returns.
insights.quote: Really inelegant if you're about to follow it up by increasing production 50% in the studio.

insights.claim: Disney+ ultimately constrains reach rather than expanding it: at ~130 million subscribers versus Netflix's ~350 million, Disney's content reaches roughly 40% of the audience it could, which matters because that content is what drives parks and merchandise demand.
insights.speaker: Ben Gilbert
insights.so_what: Reframes owned distribution as a reach tax; the counterargument the hosts weigh is that algorithmic distribution never gives any single title theatrical-style universal exposure.
insights.quote: In the Disney Plus world, Disney Plus doesn't actually give you the reach that being on the biggest streaming services would give you.

insights.claim: The hosts' conclusion after months of research is that no better alternative strategy existed: doing nothing meant consolidation or acquisition like every peer, and the winning streaming service is structurally the kitchen sink, which is incompatible with a curated prestige brand.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: If scale plus breadth is the only winning streaming configuration, then every vertical/prestige service — Peacock, Paramount+, and a boutique Disney+ — is structurally unviable standalone.
insights.quote: the winning streaming service will be the kitchen sink

themes.theme: Disney Today: Parks-Led P&L and the Bull/Bear Case

insights.claim: Bob Chapek was fired roughly two years in after a November 2022 earnings call about Disney+ losses, and the hosts argue the error was Iger recommending a caretaker for what turned out to be a wartime period of still-unresolved streaming strategy.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Succession fit is a function of the period, not the résumé — misdiagnosing peacetime versus wartime is the recurring Disney failure mode across four decades.
insights.quote: I think Iger's mistake in recommending Bob Chapek for the job was thinking that the company was about to enter a peace time.

insights.claim: Disney cumulatively absorbed roughly $13 billion of losses building Disney+ and the direct-to-consumer segment is now profitable at about $1 billion a year, which the hosts concede will probably never approach cable margins.
insights.speaker: Ben Gilbert
insights.so_what: The all-in cost of the pivot and its current run-rate return — the numerator and denominator for judging whether the streaming bet pays back.

insights.claim: Streaming is now Disney's single largest revenue source: Disney+ has 132 million subscribers, Hulu 64 million and ESPN+ 24 million, generating over $19 billion of subscription revenue as last reported in 2024 (likely ~$22 billion now), about a quarter of company revenue, up from essentially zero in 2017.
insights.speaker: Ben Gilbert
insights.so_what: Corrects the common framing of Disney+ as a money pit — it is now the revenue center of the company, just at far lower margin than what it replaced.

insights.claim: Netflix's streaming operating income of about $13.5 billion on $45 billion of revenue now equals the operating income of all of Disney combined, versus 2017 when Netflix earned under $1 billion against Disney's $14 billion.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: The single clearest measure of value transfer in media over eight years, and the empirical basis for the scale-economies argument.
insights.quote: Netflix's operating income on streaming, their entire business is the same as Disney's entire company operating income.

insights.claim: Applying Hamilton Helmer's Seven Powers, the hosts conclude Disney+ has a cornered resource versus vertical rivals like Peacock and Paramount+ but loses to Netflix purely on scale economies, and that Disney's best available position is a clear, subsidized number two rather than chasing number one.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: An actionable strategic prescription: dial back content spend, accept subscale, let the flywheel heal — the opposite of what a pure-play streamer would do.
insights.quote: I think Disney's best bet here is to be a clear number two.

insights.claim: Parks attendance is actually below its pre-pandemic peak — 145 million visitors a year versus an all-time high of 157 million — and all growth is coming from per-guest spending that has climbed roughly 5% a year for decades.
insights.speaker: Ben Gilbert
insights.so_what: Disney's best business is being grown by price, not volume, which caps long-run growth and raises the risk of eroding the mass-market brand affinity that feeds it.

insights.claim: Parks and cruises now generate almost 60% of Disney's total operating income while sports is down to 16% — a complete reversal of the situation a decade ago — which is why parks chief Josh D'Amaro was named CEO effective March 2026.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Leadership follows the P&L; expect capital allocation, org design and IP decisions to be optimized around parks demand going forward.
insights.quote: Almost 60% of the profits of the entire company come from parks and cruises.

insights.claim: Disney's current segment economics show entertainment at $42 billion of revenue producing $4.7 billion of operating income while experiences at $36 billion of revenue produces $10 billion — a physical theme park business earning twice the profit of the content business on comparable revenue.
insights.speaker: Ben Gilbert
insights.so_what: Inverts the standard assumption that digital content is higher margin than physical operations — the direct result of streaming's cost structure.

insights.claim: Theatrical distribution is only $2.6 billion of revenue, about 3% of Disney's $94 billion total, meaning the business the public identifies with Disney is economically trivial to it.
insights.speaker: Ben Gilbert
insights.so_what: The most misunderstood fact about Disney's P&L — box office matters now mainly as marketing that seeds IP for parks, merchandise and streaming.
insights.quote: From the outside, we think about the Walt Disney Company as these movies and box office. And that is not the business. That's 3% of the revenue of this company.

insights.claim: Because theme parks cannot scale on volume the way affiliate fees did — physical room and hotel capacity are fixed — Disney's $60 billion decade-long capex program (including $30 billion domestic and roughly one new cruise ship a year toward 13 ships) is what must justify continued per-guest price increases.
insights.speaker: Ben Gilbert
insights.so_what: Ties the capex cycle to the pricing strategy: the spend is the precondition for defending yield, not optional growth investment.
insights.quote: theme parks, unfortunately, don't really scale the way that cable profits did

insights.claim: The bear case is that Disney has not produced a single commercially successful new franchise since roughly 2016 — everything with big box office since Moana and Zootopia is harvesting existing IP — and that Frozen may have been the last mega hit.
insights.speaker: Ben Gilbert
insights.so_what: The key monitorable for the long thesis: new-franchise creation rate, which the hosts note coincides exactly with when streaming became king.
insights.quote: Has Disney produced a single new franchise in the last decade that has been a commercial success?

insights.claim: The second bear argument is that the Pixar, Marvel and Lucasfilm acquisitions were brilliant but provided roughly 20 years of fuel rather than 50, with Marvel possibly fully exploited and Star Wars lacking a clear next direction, while every new park attraction and sequel is tied to that same finite set.
insights.speaker: Ben Gilbert
insights.so_what: Frames the acquired IP as a depleting reserve with a measurable life, which is the strongest argument against Disney's current terminal multiple.
insights.quote: it's kind of looking like they provided amazing fuel for about 20 years, but not for 50 years

insights.claim: The bull case is that these franchises behave like luxury brands and core societal myths that cannot be killed — they cycle through highs and lows on roughly 20-year cycles, get handed down generationally, and a bad Obi-Wan show does not damage a child's first Star Wars experience.
insights.speaker: David Rosenthal
insights.so_what: The long-duration argument for owning Disney: mean-reverting IP quality with permanent brand ownership, best bought at cyclical lows.
insights.quote: I think these franchises whether it's core Disney, Pixar, Lucasfilm, Marvel are just like luxury brands. You cannot kill them.

insights.claim: Despite intentionally accelerating the decline of its most profitable legacy businesses, Disney is back at all-time-high total profits and on track for a record net income in 2026 — though at a 3-5% growth rate that will not support a high multiple.
insights.speaker: Ben Gilbert
insights.so_what: The valuation crux: record absolute profits with low growth argues for treating Disney as a mature cash-return story rather than a growth compounder.

insights.claim: David Rosenthal's pitch for Disney's next acquisitions is Bluey — a Pixar-like creative asset that cannot scale standalone under Joe Brumm and is already quasi-inside Disney — and Nintendo, whose market cap has fallen 50% in a year to about $50 billion, making it cheaper than Fox despite owning Mario, Zelda and Pokémon.
insights.speaker: David Rosenthal
insights.so_what: A concrete, checkable investment idea: Nintendo as the last unowned tier-A IP portfolio, though the hosts flag Japan would likely never allow a sale.
insights.quote: Nintendo is like Pixar, Marvel, and Lucasfilm combined.

insights.claim: Ben Gilbert's closing thesis is that Disney's 1990s and 2005-2019 prosperity was a structural anomaly created by an unusually favorable environment — cable bundle autopilot profits, frequent moviegoing and high-margin home video — and that the company will be permanently and unfairly compared against it.
insights.speaker: Ben Gilbert
insights.so_what: The right baseline for evaluating current management: not the historical peak, but what any operator could earn in today's structurally worse media environment.
insights.quote: the prosperity from the late 90s and the 2005 to 2019 era, that was a complete anomaly due to how good all the structural forces around the business were

insights.claim: The hosts argue the modern content environment is far worse for producers but the best ever for consumers, with all streaming services combined costing roughly what a single cable bundle used to cost while offering vastly more choice.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Consumer surplus expanded while producer surplus collapsed — the general condition to expect in any market where distribution costs go to zero.
insights.quote: It's a it's the best deal ever for consumers.

insights.claim: Bob Iger's 20-year tenure roughly 5x'd the stock, tripled revenue from $31 billion to $94 billion and 5x'd net income from $2.5 billion to $12.4 billion — profit outpacing revenue, the same pattern as under Eisner, which the hosts say says more about how bad 1984 Disney was than about the last 40 years.
insights.speaker: Acquired host
insights.so_what: Both celebrated CEO eras were margin-expansion stories off a depressed base, which sets realistic expectations for D'Amaro from today's already-optimized starting point.
